## Introduction

R makes it remarkably easy to fit a multivariate linear model. You don't need a special
function. You just give `lm()` a matrix of responses instead of a single one:

```{r}
#| label: fit
#| code-fold: false
fit <- lm(cbind(mpg, qsec) ~ hp + wt, data = mtcars)
class(fit)
```

<!--
mtcars is just for the hook: two responses, fuel economy and quarter-mile time.
A better-motivated example (Rohwer? iris? NeuroCog?) can take over in the package
sections. Or use one dataset throughout?
-->

The result is an object of class `"mlm"` that *also* inherits from `"lm"`. That second
class is a promise, or at least a hope: anything that works for a linear model should work
here too. So, as you would for any regression, you ask for the diagnostic plots:

```{r}
#| label: plot-fails
#| code-fold: false
#| error: true
plot(fit)
```

Well, that's honest, at least. Other functions fail less gracefully. Several old friends from
the `car` package stop with messages that tell you nothing about why:

```{r}
#| label: car-fails
#| code-fold: false
#| error: true
car::avPlots(fit)
car::vif(fit)
```

The more interesting cases are the ones that ** *don't* fail**, but don't give you anything **useful**:
`cooks.distance()` runs without a
murmur and gives you a Cook's D for each case, separately for each response:

```{r}
#| label: cooks-quiet
#| code-fold: false
head(cooks.distance(fit), 4)
```

That's two **univariate** answers to what was a **multivariate** question: which cases have an undue
influence on the model as a whole? 

* `summary(fit)` does the same thing, returning a list of
separate regression summaries, one per response, as if you'd called `lm()` twice. 
* Nothing
warns you that the correlation between the responses, which is the whole point of fitting
them together, has dropped out of the analysis. 

The question of _multivariate influence_
is now largely solved in my [`mvinfluence`](https://friendly.github.io/mvinfluence/) package, which was part of my learning curve
for the larger question I'm addressing here.

In short, the multivariate linear model is **easy to fit** and **hard to see**. 

* The model syntax in `lm()` is trivial & expressive: `y` becomes `cbind(y1, y2, ...)`. You only need to
  understand the idea of **"binding"** rows or columns into a matrix. But the `cbind` base family
  also works for a sequence of vectors, matrices and dataframes. 
* The matrix algebra extension is elegant & beautiful:
  $\mathbf{y}_{n \times 1} \rightarrow \mathbf{Y}_{n \times q}$ --- it largely just works!
  The residual variance $\sigma^2$ becomes a covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$. The
  $F$ ratio of hypothesis to error sums of squares becomes the eigenvalues of
  $\mathbf{H}\mathbf{E}^{-1}$, which give Wilks' $\Lambda$, the Pillai trace,
  Hotelling-Lawley and their friend Roy. And
  $\textrm{Var}(\widehat{\mathbf{b}}) = \sigma^2 (\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X})^{-1}$ becomes
  $\textrm{Var}(\textrm{vec}\, \widehat{\mathbf{B}}) = \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \otimes (\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X})^{-1}$.
  Once there's a covariance matrix, you can even ask whether it's the same in every group:
  Box's $\mathcal{M}$ test [#ref: Box:1949 in statistics.bib].

@fig-techniques puts
this in a wider frame. It classifies the familiar linear-model methods by the number and kind
of predictors and responses. For one response ($q = 1$), we have a rich toolkit of graphical
methods: added-variable plots, influence plots, effect plots and the rest. For several
quantitative responses ($q > 1$), the methods are just as well developed on the statistical
side (multivariate regression, MANOVA, canonical correlation), but the graphics have been
thin. Mostly, the results arrive as tables of multivariate test statistics.

![Techniques for linear models, classified by the number of predictors ($p$) and responses
($q$), and whether these are quantitative or discrete. The $q > 1$ columns are where
graphical methods have been thin. *Source*: [Visualizing Multivariate Data and Models in
R](https://friendly.github.io/Vis-MLM-book), Figure 6.1.](figures/techniques-table.png){#fig-techniques width="90%" fig-alt="A table of linear-model techniques. Rows: predictors, quantitative or discrete, with p = 1 or p > 1. Columns: responses, quantitative or discrete, with q = 1 or q > 1. For quantitative responses, simple and multiple regression, t-test and ANOVA (q = 1) generalize to multivariate regression, canonical and partial correlation, Hotelling T-squared and MANOVA (q > 1). For discrete responses, logistic regression, chi-square, discriminant analysis, logit and loglinear models."}

## One more dimension

Why should this be so hard? The statistics of the multivariate linear model have been
settled for more than half a century. The trouble is more mundane, and I think it's worth
naming, because it explains nearly every problem I've run into in developing these ideas.

It calls to mind the cognitive problems "A. Square" encountered in Edwin Abbott's
_Flatland_ [#ref], when a Sphere entered the story and taught him how to think in
one more dimension. I've told that story in my[ _Visualizing Multivariate Data and Models in R_]() book. 

In R, when the response goes from a vector **y** to a matrix **Y**, every object the model produces
**gains a dimension**:

* a **scalar becomes a vector, or a matrix**. The residual variance $\sigma^2$ becomes a
  $q \times q$ covariance matrix $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$.
* a **vector becomes a matrix**. The coefficients $\mathbf{b}$ become a $p \times q$ matrix
  $\mathbf{B}$, and the residuals become an $n \times q$ matrix.
* a **matrix becomes a 3-way array**, or a list of matrices. A table of confidence intervals
  for the coefficients ($p \times 2$) becomes $p \times 2 \times q$. The standard error of each
  fitted value becomes a $q \times q$ matrix, one for every case.

@fig-dimension-ladder shows this ladder for a model with $p = 3$ coefficients and $q = 2$
responses.

![Going from `lm` to `mlm`, every object gains a dimension. Blue cells are what a univariate
model gives you; orange cells are added by the second response. The residual for a case
becomes a vector, the coefficient vector becomes a matrix, and the table of confidence
intervals becomes a 3-way array.](figures/dimension-ladder.png){#fig-dimension-ladder width="75%" fig-alt="A three-row diagram. Left column, lm with one response: a single cell for the residual e_i, a column of three cells for the coefficients b, and a 3 by 2 grid for their confidence intervals. Right column, mlm with q responses: each object gains orange cells along a new dimension, becoming a 1 by 2 vector, a 3 by 2 matrix B, and a 3 by 2 by 2 array drawn as two stacked layers."}

<!-- Drawn by R/dimension-ladder.R (run from this folder). Possible additions: a fourth
rung for sigma^2 -> Sigma (scalar -> matrix, skipping a rung), or se.fit. -->

That extra dimension shows up first in what a function *returns*, and then in every method that
has to consume it: `print()`, `summary()`, `confint()`, `predict()`, and of course `plot()`.

Code written for one shape is handed the next one up. But this has to do *something* with the
new `dim(X) + 1` object. The challenge has always been: How to do something more **useful**
in a multivariate context.


Base R takes several different approaches. Sometimes it simply returns the bigger object:
`coef(fit)` is the $3 \times 2$ matrix you'd expect. Sometimes it **flattens** the extra
dimension away. `confint()` strings the responses and coefficients together into one long
list of intervals:

```{r}
#| label: confint-flat
#| code-fold: false
confint(fit)
```

The `broom` package does much the same thing in tidy form, stacking the responses in a
long data frame with a `response` column. That's perfectly convenient for a table, but in both
cases the answers for `mpg` and `qsec` sit side by side as if they had nothing to do with
each other.

And sometimes R just **refuses**, as it currently does in for the `predict()` generic:

```{r}
#| label: predict-refuses
#| code-fold: false
#| error: true
predict(fit, newdata = mtcars[1:2, ], se.fit = TRUE)
```

I have some sympathy for that last one. 

* For a univariate model, the standard error of a
predicted value is a single number, and a confidence interval is a pair of numbers, `lwr` and
`upr`. 

* For an `mlm`, the uncertainty of each predicted point is a $q \times q$ covariance
matrix, and the natural confidence region is an *ellipse* (an ellipsoid when $q > 2$) around it. What should `predict()` return? How should it print? There's no column in
`cbind(fit, lwr, upr)` for an ellipse. Work on this is still unfinished in `heplots`
(`dev/pred.mlm.R`)

<!--
predict.mlm() is an unfinished item in heplots (dev/pred.mlm.R returns an n x q x 3
array). Mention here briefly, or save it for "What's still missing"? I'd keep a
one-sentence pointer here and the details at the end.
-->

So here's the argument of this post, in a nutshell:

::: {.thesis}
> A good multivariate extension isn't just "run the univariate method $q$ times". It has to
> decide what to do with the extra dimension: find the matrix that plays the role of the
> scalar, and then find a way to see it. Most often, as it turns out, that way is an ellipse.
:::

<!--
That's the thesis line. Alternative endings for that last sentence:
  - "...and very often, the picture of that matrix is an ellipse."
  - tie to Elliptical Insights (Friendly, Monette & Fox, 2013) here or later.
-->

## Filling in the gaps

Over the past twenty years or so I've been filling these gaps, one package at a time, often
with John Fox and Georges Monette:

<!-- CHECK: co-authors per package, and approximate start dates (from NEWS/DESCRIPTION).
     Is a personal-history thread wanted here, or keep it impersonal? -->

* [**heplots**](https://friendly.github.io/heplots/) shows multivariate hypothesis tests as
  ellipses: the HE plot.
* [**candisc**](https://friendly.github.io/candisc/) finds the low-dimensional view in which
  those tests are easiest to see.
* [**mvinfluence**](https://friendly.github.io/mvinfluence/) generalizes leverage and Cook's
  distance to multivariate models.
* `heplots::robmlm()` fits a robust version, downweighting cases with large residuals.
* [**genridge**](https://friendly.github.io/genridge/), my package for visualizing ridge
  regression, is now (in its development version) learning to handle a matrix of responses.

<!-- verify the pkgdown URLs before publishing -->

Each one is a case of the same problem: deciding what the extra dimension means, for the
statistics and for the software. The sections below take them in turn.

## Seeing the tests: HE plots

In a univariate linear model, every $F$ test compares two sums of squares: $SS_H$ for the
hypothesis and $SS_E$ for error. In the multivariate model, each of these becomes a
$q \times q$ matrix of sums of squares and products: $\mathbf{H}$ for each term in the
model, and one $\mathbf{E}$ for the residuals. All four multivariate test statistics are
functions of the eigenvalues of $\mathbf{H}\mathbf{E}^{-1}$, the matrix analog of
$SS_H / SS_E$.

That's the matrix that plays the role of the scalar. The way to see it is the **HE plot**
(Friendly, 2007; Fox, Friendly & Monette, 2009): draw $\mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{E}$ as
ellipses in the space of two responses. The $\mathbf{E}$ ellipse shows the size and shape
of the residual variation. The $\mathbf{H}$ ellipse for a term shows the variation of the
fitted values due to that term. With the default "evidence" scaling, $\mathbf{H}$
protrudes outside $\mathbf{E}$ somewhere in the full response space if and only if the
term is significant by Roy's test. (In a two-dimensional view, the rule works only one
way: outside means significant, but inside doesn't mean "not significant".)

Here's an example, from Rohwer's study of how well paired-associate (PA) learning tasks
predict three aptitude and achievement tests in kindergarten children of high and low
socioeconomic status (SES). The model is a multivariate analysis of covariance: SES
is a factor, and the five PA tasks are covariates.

```{r}
#| label: rohwer-mod
library(heplots)
data(Rohwer, package = "heplots")
rohwer.mod <- lm(cbind(SAT, PPVT, Raven) ~ SES + n + s + ns + na + ss, data = Rohwer)
car::Anova(rohwer.mod)
```

The `heplot()` below shows the $\mathbf{H}$ ellipses for all six terms in the space of
`SAT` and `PPVT`, plus one more, `Regr`, for the joint hypothesis that all five PA
coefficients are zero.

```{r}
#| label: fig-rohwer-heplot
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: "75%"
#| fig-cap: "HE plot for the Rohwer MANCOVA model, in the space of SAT and PPVT. Each 1-df term is a line; the `Regr` ellipse tests all five PA tasks together. Terms whose H ellipse or line extends outside the E ellipse are significant."
#| fig-alt: "HE plot of PPVT against SAT. A red dashed Error ellipse is centered at the grand mean. A large green Regr ellipse, tilted upward, extends well outside it. Lines for SES, na and ns also extend outside the Error ellipse; the lines for n, s and ss stay inside. Points mark the Hi and Lo SES group means."
# colors: Error first, then the six terms, then the Regr hypothesis
col <- c("red", "darkgreen", "blue", "cyan3", "magenta", "brown", "darkgray", "purple")
heplot(rohwer.mod,
       hypotheses = list("Regr" = c("n", "s", "ns", "na", "ss")),
       col = col, fill = TRUE, fill.alpha = 0.1)
```

The plot tells most of the story of the `Anova()` table at a glance. SES and `na`
extend beyond $\mathbf{E}$, while `n`, `s` and `ss` stay well inside. `ns`, also
significant, only just reaches the edge of $\mathbf{E}$ in this view: the one-way rule at
work. The tilt of the
`Regr` ellipse shows that the PA tasks predict `SAT` and `PPVT` together, in the same
direction. There's also a lesson about shape. Each term with 1 df has an $\mathbf{H}$
matrix of rank 1, so its "ellipse" collapses to a line. In general, the dimension of the
$\mathbf{H}$ ellipse is the smaller of the term's df and $q$.

### What was easy

The `heplot()` functions were, honestly, the easy part, because the statistics were
already done. John Fox's `car::Anova()` computes $\mathbf{H}$ for every term, and
`car::linearHypothesis()` does so for any linear hypothesis. `Anova()` returns these as a
*list* of $q \times q$ matrices, one per term: the "list of matrices" rung of the ladder.
So `heplot.mlm()` is "only" a plot method on that list:

* choose two (or three) responses and take the corresponding submatrices of
  $\mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{E}$;
* scale them (by the error df, and for evidence scaling, by the critical value of Roy's
  test);
* draw each one as an ellipse, using its Cholesky factor to transform a circle.

Everything that `Anova()` can test, `heplot()` can draw, including repeated-measures
designs through its `idata` and `idesign` arguments. And because `heplot()` is an S3
generic, anything that inherits from `"mlm"` gets an HE plot for free.

The **same design** S3 design principle in R gave a family of graphical methods for `"mlm"` objects: `pairs()` for all pairs of
responses, `heplot3d()` for three, and `heplot1d()` for one. Other helpers came along:

* `coefplot()` shows confidence ellipses for the coefficients, generalizing
  `car::confidenceEllipse()`;
* `cqplot()` is a $\chi^2$ QQ plot of the squared Mahalanobis distances of the residuals;
* `etasq()` gives multivariate measures of effect size, and `glance()` a
  `broom`-style one-row summary for each response.

The [MANOVA](https://friendly.github.io/heplots/articles/HE_manova.html) and
[MMRA](https://friendly.github.io/heplots/articles/HE_mmra.html) vignettes have many more
examples.

## Seeing it in fewer dimensions: candisc

An HE plot shows two responses at a time, and `pairs()` shows all of them, two at a time.
But the effect of a term doesn't have to line up with any pair of responses. The
$\mathbf{H}$ ellipsoid for a term lives in $s = \min(q, df_h)$ dimensions, in directions
that are combinations of all the responses.

The eigenvectors of $\mathbf{H}\mathbf{E}^{-1}$ point in those directions. They define the
*canonical variates*: linear combinations of the responses that are uncorrelated within
groups, ordered by how much of the effect they capture. Their eigenvalues are the same
ones that go into the multivariate test statistics. So the canonical space is the
low-dimensional view in which the test is easiest to see.

The `Pottery` data give an example: the chemical composition (five oxides) of ancient
pottery from four sites in Britain. With $q = 5$ responses and $df_h = 3$ for `Site`, the
effect lives in $s = 3$ dimensions. `candisc()` finds them:

```{r}
#| label: pottery-can
library(candisc)
data(Pottery, package = "carData")
pottery.mlm <- lm(cbind(Al, Fe, Mg, Ca, Na) ~ Site, data = Pottery)
pottery.can <- candisc(pottery.mlm)
pottery.can
```

The first dimension accounts for 96% of the differences among the sites, and only the
first two are significant. A two-dimensional plot of the canonical space shows nearly
everything:

```{r}
#| label: fig-pottery-can
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: "75%"
#| fig-cap: "HE plot of the Pottery data in canonical space. In this view, the E ellipse is a circle. Arrows show the correlations of the oxides with the canonical dimensions."
#| fig-alt: "Canonical HE plot, Can2 (3.5%) against Can1 (96.4%). The Site H ellipse is long and flat along Can1; the red Error ellipse is a small circle at the origin. Isle Thorns and Ashley Rails lie at the left, Llanedyrn and Caldicot at the right, with Caldicot lower. Arrows for Fe, Mg and Ca point right, Al points left, and Na points up and to the right."
heplot(pottery.can, var.lwd = 2, fill = TRUE, fill.alpha = 0.1)
```

The plot is a kind of biplot for the HE plot. The $\mathbf{E}$ ellipse becomes a circle,
because the canonical variates are uncorrelated within groups and scaled to have equal
error variance. Directions in this space are therefore comparable, and the size of
$\mathbf{H}$ relative to the circle shows the strength of the effect. The arrows show how
each oxide is correlated with the canonical dimensions. Here, `Can1` is mainly a contrast
of aluminum against iron, magnesium and calcium, which separates Isle Thorns and Ashley
Rails from Llanedyrn and Caldicot.

In terms of the ladder, `candisc()` doesn't need to ignore the extra dimensions; it
*rotates* them. It finds the directions that matter for one term, and lets you ignore the
rest knowing how little you lose.

The software followed the heplots design. `candisc()` gets $\mathbf{H}$ and $\mathbf{E}$
from the same `car::Anova()` call, and returns a `"candisc"` object, for which there are
`heplot()`, `heplot3d()` and `plot()` methods. `candiscList()` does this for every term in
the model. `can_lm()` goes one step further, refitting the model with the canonical scores
as responses. And `varOrder()` uses the angles of those arrows to order the responses in
other displays, like `pairs()`, so that related variables sit together.

## Influence: mvinfluence

In the introduction, `cooks.distance(fit)` quietly gave two univariate answers, one column
per response. Load mvinfluence, and the same call gives one answer per case:

```{r}
#| label: cooks-mv
#| code-fold: false
library(mvinfluence)
head(cooks.distance(fit), 4)
```

The math came from Barrett & Ling (1992). Their generalized Cook's distance strings the
coefficient matrix out into one long vector, $\textrm{vec}(\mathbf{B})$, and measures how
far it moves when a case is deleted, in the metric of its covariance matrix. That metric is
$\mathbf{S}^{-1} \otimes \mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X}$: the Kronecker product again. As in
the univariate case, $D_i$ is proportional to the product of a leverage component and a
residual component. Leverage depends only on $\mathbf{X}$, so it doesn't change. The
residual is now a vector, so its size becomes
$q_{ii} = \mathbf{e}_i^\top (\mathbf{E}^\top \mathbf{E})^{-1} \mathbf{e}_i$, a hat value
for the residuals: one more scalar that has become a quadratic form.

Is the multivariate version worth the trouble? Barrett (2003) gave a toy example, with one
predictor and two nearly identical responses, that makes the case:

```{r}
#| label: toy
Toy <- data.frame(
  x  = c(1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 10),
  y1 = c(0.10, 1.90, 1.00, 2.95, 2.10, 4.00, 2.95, 4.95, 10.00),
  y2 = c(0.10, 1.80, 1.00, 2.93, 2.00, 4.10, 3.05, 4.93, 10.00)
)
Toy.mlm <- lm(cbind(y1, y2) ~ x, data = Toy)
data.frame(D1  = cooks.distance(lm(y1 ~ x, data = Toy)),
           D2  = cooks.distance(lm(y2 ~ x, data = Toy)),
           D12 = cooks.distance(Toy.mlm)) |> round(3)
```

Case 9, at $x = 10$, has high leverage, but it lies right on the line for each response, so
its univariate Cook's distances are tiny. Its multivariate $D$ is more than ten times
that of any other case. Because `y1` and `y2` are so highly correlated, the covariance
matrix of the coefficients is nearly singular, and small discrepancies in case 9's
position, invisible to either regression alone, are magnified in the joint fit. The
[vignette](https://friendly.github.io/mvinfluence/articles/uni-vs-multi.html) works
through this example in detail.

### Design challenges

Barrett & Ling's measures go further than single cases. They're defined for deleting any
*subset* $I$ of $m$ cases, which matters because pairs of influential cases can mask each
other, or have a joint influence far beyond their individual ones (Lawrence, 1995).
For a subset, the leverage and residual quantities $\mathbf{H}_I$ and $\mathbf{Q}_I$ are
$m \times m$ matrices. That's the ladder once more, and it set the design:

* **The structure follows stats.** As `influence.lm()` calls `lm.influence()`,
  `influence.mlm()` is a thin wrapper around `mlm.influence()`, which does the work. With
  `hatvalues()` and `cooks.distance()` methods for `"mlm"`, the familiar generic functions
  just work.
* **The results are lists of matrices**, one for each of the $\binom{n}{m}$ subsets. To
  plot or sort them, you need a scalar, so the functions take an argument `FUN`, either
  `det()` or `tr()`, for the "size" of each matrix. For $m = 1$, the two agree.
* **Each subset is refit directly.** The coefficients and residuals for each deleted subset
  come from direct matrix calculation, rather than from the QR decomposition that
  `lm.influence()` uses. That's simple, but the number of subsets grows quickly with $m$.
* **Barrett & Ling unify many measures** (Cook's $D$, DFFITS, and others) as the trace or
  determinant of products like
  $\mathbf{H}_I \mathbf{Q}_I (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{H}_I - \mathbf{Q}_I)^a (\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{H}_I)^b$.
  Computing these needs powers of matrices, so the package has `mpower()` and a `%^%`
  operator.

### New influence plots

The univariate influence plot in **car** shows studentized residuals against hat values,
with bubbles whose area is proportional to Cook's distance. `influencePlot()` for an
`"mlm"` does the same with the multivariate measures. It also offers a second form,
`type = "LR"`, adapting an idea from McCulloch & Meeter (1983). Because $D$ is proportional
to the product $L \times R$ of the leverage and residual components, a plot of
$\log R$ against $\log L$ turns contours of constant Cook's distance into straight lines
with slope $-1$. Adjacent lines mark constant *multiples* of influence.

```{r}
#| label: fig-toy-influence
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-cap: "Multivariate influence plots for the toy example. Left: squared studentized residual against hat value. Right: the LR form, log residual component against log leverage component; the dashed diagonal lines are contours of constant Cook's distance. Bubble areas are proportional to the generalized Cook's D."
#| fig-alt: "Two bubble plots. In both, cases 1, 2 and 6 and the other small cases sit at the lower left with tiny bubbles, and case 9 is a large red bubble at the upper right. In the right panel, dashed diagonal lines of slope minus one run across the plot, and case 9 lies several contours beyond all the other cases."
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1) + 0.1)
influencePlot(Toy.mlm, id.n = 2, scale = 5,
              xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1.3))
influencePlot(Toy.mlm, id.n = 2, scale = 5, type = "LR",
              xlim = c(-2.5, 2.5), ylim = c(-2, 2.6))
par(op)
```

In the LR plot, case 9 lies several contours beyond every other case, and its position shows
why: it's extreme in *both* leverage and residual. The same plot works for univariate
models too, as `lrPlot()`.

## Robustness: robmlm()

For a univariate model, `MASS::rlm()` gives a robust fit, downweighting cases with large
residuals. Give it a matrix response, and it stops with "incompatible dimensions".

The algorithm for a multivariate version, `heplots::robmlm()`, is short. It's iteratively
reweighted least squares, with one change, which is the ladder again. In `rlm()`, a case's
weight depends on the size of its residual, $|e_i| / s$, a scalar. Here the residual is a
vector, so its size becomes a squared Mahalanobis distance, $\mathbf{e}_i^\top
\mathbf{S}^{-1} \mathbf{e}_i$, using a robust estimate of the residual covariance matrix
$\mathbf{S}$ from `MASS::cov.trob()`. Bisquare weights are computed from these distances,
with a cutoff from the $\chi^2_q$ distribution, and the model is refit by weighted least
squares until the coefficients stop changing.

### What took more work

The harder part was making the result a full citizen of the `"mlm"` world. A `robmlm`
object has class `c("robmlm", "mlm", "lm")`, so `car::Anova()`, `heplot()` and the rest
should accept it. But the weights got in the way. Ask base R for the covariance matrix of a
weighted `mlm`, and it refuses:
`'mlm' objects with weights are not supported`. So heplots provides its own
`vcov.mlm()`, which takes the weights into account.

That works, but it's a sharp tool. Once heplots is loaded, its method replaces the one in
**stats** for *every* `"mlm"` object, not just robust ones. It gives the same answers when
there are no weights, but it's the kind of design choice I'd think twice about today.
Smaller things came later. `robmlm()` now has a method for an `mlm` object, so you can
write `robmlm(mod)` instead of repeating the formula and data, and it stores its call, so
`update()` works.

Then there were the visualizations. What does a robust fit change, and how can you see
it? `plot()` for a `robmlm` object shows the final weights for each case. Overlaying the HE
plots for the classical and robust fits shows what the downweighting does to the test.
Here it is for the `Pottery` model from the candisc section.

```{r}
#| label: pottery-fits
pottery.rlm <- robmlm(pottery.mlm)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-pottery-robust
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: "Robust MANOVA for the Pottery data. Left: final case weights from `robmlm()`, colored by site. Right: HE plots for the classical (blue, solid) and robust (red, dashed) fits, for Al and Fe."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels. Left: an index plot of case weights. Most are near 1, but cases 1, 7, 11 and 25 have weights near 0, and cases 9 and 10 about 0.5. Right: HE plot of Fe against Al. The classical and robust Site ellipses nearly coincide, a long thin ellipse running from upper left to lower right. The robust Error ellipse is clearly smaller than the classical one."
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1) + 0.1)
plot(pottery.rlm, col = Pottery$Site, segments = TRUE)

heplot(pottery.mlm, variables = c("Al", "Fe"),
       col = c("blue", "blue"), fill = TRUE, fill.alpha = 0.1)
heplot(pottery.rlm, variables = c("Al", "Fe"), add = TRUE, error.ellipse = TRUE,
       col = c("red", "red"), fill = TRUE, fill.alpha = 0.1, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("Classical", "Robust"), col = c("blue", "red"),
       lty = 1:2, lwd = 2, bty = "n")
par(op)
```

Four cases (1, 7, 11 and 25) get weights near zero, and two more (9 and 10) about one half.
The robust $\mathbf{H}$ ellipse for `Site` is nearly the same as the classical one, but the
$\mathbf{E}$ ellipse shrinks. Downweighting a few unusual pots makes the differences among
sites stand out more: the $F$ for Pillai's test rises from 4.3 to 6.6. The
[Robust vignette](https://friendly.github.io/heplots/articles/Robust.html) has the details,
and a second example with a multivariate regression.

## What's still missing

### Not done yet: `predict.mlm()` with standard errors

Back in the introduction, `predict(fit, se.fit = TRUE)` simply refused. The statistics
aren't hard. For a new case with predictors $\mathbf{x}_0$, the predicted response vector
is $\hat{\mathbf{y}}_0^\top = \mathbf{x}_0^\top \widehat{\mathbf{B}}$, and its covariance
matrix is $h_0 \widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$, where
$h_0 = \mathbf{x}_0^\top (\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X})^{-1} \mathbf{x}_0$ is its leverage.
The standard error has become a $q \times q$ matrix, and the confidence interval has become
a confidence *ellipse*, with a radius from Hotelling's $T^2$:
$c^2 = \frac{q (n-p)}{n-p-q+1} F_{q,\, n-p-q+1}(0.95)$.
For a prediction ellipse, which includes the error for a new case, $h_0$ becomes
$1 + h_0$.

Here's what that looks like for three hypothetical cars, using the `mtcars` model from the
introduction:

```{r}
#| label: fig-pred-ellipses
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 5
#| out-width: "65%"
#| fig-cap: "95% confidence ellipses (blue) and prediction ellipses (red, dashed) for the predicted (mpg, qsec) of three new cars from the `mtcars` model. All have the shape of the residual covariance matrix; only their size changes, with each car's leverage."
#| fig-alt: "Scatterplot of qsec against mpg for the mtcars data, in gray. Three small filled blue ellipses mark the confidence regions for three predicted points, at about (14, 16), (21, 17.5) and (26, 18). Much larger dashed red prediction ellipses surround each one. All six ellipses have the same orientation, tilted slightly upward."
new <- data.frame(hp = c(100, 150, 250), wt = c(2, 3, 4))
X  <- model.matrix(fit)
X0 <- model.matrix(~ hp + wt, new)
n <- nrow(X); p <- ncol(X); q <- 2
Sigma <- crossprod(residuals(fit)) / (n - p)
h0    <- rowSums((X0 %*% solve(crossprod(X))) * X0)   # leverage of each new case
c2    <- q * (n - p) / (n - p - q + 1) * qf(0.95, q, n - p - q + 1)
yhat  <- predict(fit, new)

plot(qsec ~ mpg, data = mtcars, col = "gray50", pch = 16,
     xlim = c(5, 35), ylim = c(13, 24))
for (i in seq_len(nrow(new))) {
  car::ellipse(yhat[i, ], h0[i] * Sigma, sqrt(c2),
               col = "blue", fill = TRUE, lwd = 2, center.pch = 3)
  car::ellipse(yhat[i, ], (1 + h0[i]) * Sigma, sqrt(c2),
               col = "red", lty = 2, lwd = 1, center.pch = NULL)
}
```

Every ellipse has the shape of $\widehat{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$; only the size changes. So
the math fits in a dozen lines. What's not settled is the software, and that's the extra
dimension again:

* **What should it return?** `predict.lm()` returns `fit`, `lwr` and `upr` as columns of a
  matrix. A draft in heplots returns an $n \times q \times 3$ array of per-response bounds,
  roughly the shadows of the ellipse on each axis, not the ellipse itself. The full
  answer is an $n \times q \times q$ array of covariance matrices.
* **How should it print?** Nobody wants to read $n$ covariance matrices.
* **How should it plot?** Probably as above, which puts it back in heplots territory.
